facts.text: The Ifugao rice terraces are in the mountains of the northern Philippines, at roughly 800 to 1,500 meters above sea level.
The terraces were built, and are still kept up, by the Ifugao people.
FAO (the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization) designated the Ifugao Rice Terraces a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System in 2011.
The terraces were added to the World Heritage List in 1995 as a living cultural landscape.
The muyong are small woodlots owned privately by families or clans and passed down as inherited property.
Sitting above the terraces, the woodlots catch rainwater and nutrients and release them slowly to the fields below.
The terraces are kept flooded all year, which requires healthy woodlots to supply enough water.
Rice is grown once a year, but after the harvest farmers grow vegetables on organic mounds and beds and raise fish in holes inside the terraces.
Tinawon, the local heirloom rice, takes its name from a word meaning once a year; it is planted and harvested only once a year.
Tinawon is aromatic and organically grown, can sell for a high price, and according to IRRI is found in only three places in the world.
The terraces are widely described as about 2,000 years old; FAO’s GIAHS page gives this figure.
The UCLA-led Ifugao Archaeological Project found that wet-rice farming appeared and spread rapidly in the highlands soon after Spanish colonization reached the region around AD 1600.
The project sees the upland rice fields as a response to social and political pressure from Spanish colonization, showing that indigenous groups were not passive under colonial rule.
The terraces’ age has long been debated: one older theory says about 2,000 years, another about 400 years, and carbon dates differ from place to place.
Many young Ifugao have moved away because terrace farming seems to offer few economic opportunities, leaving older parents to look after the terraces.
The elders left behind may be the last people who know how to maintain the terrace walls and irrigation.
Because of the labor shortage, major damage caused by natural disasters is sometimes left unrepaired.
Earthworm infestation adds to erosion and can make terrace walls and dikes collapse.
Some terraces have been turned into commercial vegetable farms or built on, and others have been abandoned for better-paid work.

Some farmers earn extra money from tourism: an elderly farmer featured by FAO guides visitors through the terraces; guests can stay overnight, eat traditional rice dishes, and a few help with planting and harvesting.
